grammar.explanation: Attach ~으면 to stems ending in a consonant and ~면 to stems ending in a vowel or ㄹ. The first clause is the condition and the second says what will happen once it is met; whether English says "when" or "if" depends on how certain the condition is. Irregulars change as usual before 으: ㅂ becomes 우 (추우면), ㄷ becomes ㄹ (들으면), ㅅ drops (나으면), and ㅎ drops (그러면).

examples.ko: 비가 오면 빨래를 안 할 거예요.
examples.en: If it rains, I won't do the laundry.

examples.ko: 내일 시간이 있으면 같이 영화를 봐요.
examples.en: If you have time tomorrow, let's watch a movie.
When the signal changes, cross the street.
If the weather is cold, I will stay home.

grammar.explanation: The same ending can state a general cause and effect that anyone would expect, or a habit that repeats every time the first action happens. Because these are not one-off future events, the final clause is normally in the present tense, and "whenever" or "every time" is often the best translation.

examples.en: When winter comes, the weather gets cold.

examples.ko: 습도가 높으면 빨래가 잘 안 말라요.
examples.en: When the humidity is high, laundry doesn't dry well.
Whenever I am tired, I drink coffee.

examples.ko: 콜라를 많이 마시면 잠을 잘 못 자요.
examples.en: If I drink a lot of cola, I can't sleep well.

grammar.explanation: Putting the condition in the past tense (~았/었으면) imagines a situation that did not actually happen. The result clause usually ends in ~았/었을 것이다 (spoken ~았/었을 거예요) to mean "would have". ~았/었더라면 can replace ~았/었으면 with the same meaning.

examples.ko: 어제 일찍 잤으면 오늘 피곤하지 않았을 거예요.
examples.en: If I had slept early yesterday, I wouldn't be tired today.

examples.ko: 우산이 있었으면 비를 맞지 않았을 거예요.
examples.en: If I had had an umbrella, I wouldn't have gotten rained on.

examples.ko: 그 남자가 수상하지 않았으면 문을 열었을 거예요.
examples.en: If that man hadn't been suspicious, I would have opened the door.

grammar.explanation: First conjugate the word into the plain/diary form, then add ~면: verbs become ~ㄴ/는다면 (간다면, 먹는다면), adjectives just ~다면 (좋다면), past tense ~았/었다면, and 이다 becomes ~(이)라면. It means the same as ~(으)면 but stresses that the condition is only a hypothesis, so "if" is the usual translation.

examples.ko: 내일 날씨가 좋다면 공원에 갈 거예요.
examples.en: If the weather is nice tomorrow, I'll go to the park.

examples.ko: 제가 과학자가 된다면 습도를 연구하고 싶어요.
examples.en: If I became a scientist, I would want to study humidity.

examples.ko: 돈이 많다면 큰 집을 살 거예요.
examples.en: If I had a lot of money, I would buy a big house.

examples.ko: 제가 너라면 그 사람을 믿지 않을 거야.
examples.en: If I were you, I wouldn't trust that person.

grammar.explanation: 만약 has no direct meaning of its own; it is placed at the start of a conditional sentence to signal that a supposition is coming. It is very common together with ~(으)면 and ~ㄴ/는다면.

examples.ko: 만약 내일 비바람이 오면 경기가 취소될 거예요.
examples.en: If there is a rainstorm tomorrow, the game will be cancelled.
If I am late, go ahead first.

examples.ko: 만약 돈이 있었으면 그 집을 샀을 거예요.
examples.en: If I had had money, I would have bought that house.

grammar.explanation: Adding ~(으)면 or ~다면 to 그렇다 gives 그러면 and 그렇다면, meaning "if so" or "in that case" in response to a situation just mentioned. 아니다 + ~면 gives 아니면, "if not / otherwise", and between two nouns it works like "or".

examples.en: In that case, let's meet tomorrow.
If so, I won't go either.

examples.ko: 빨리 진정하세요. 아니면 콜라를 안 줄 거예요.
examples.en: Calm down quickly. Otherwise I won't give you a cola.

examples.ko: 저는 커피 아니면 콜라를 마시고 싶어요.
examples.en: I want to drink coffee or cola.

vocab.en: to back out on, to betray
to turn on (music, TV, tap, AC)
to write up, to fill out

grammar.explanation: Add ~자 to any verb stem, with or without a final consonant and with no irregular changes, to suggest doing something together. It is informal and cannot take ~요, so use it only with friends or people younger than you. "Let's not" is ~지 말자.

examples.en: Let's eat together.
Let's rest at home today.
Let's not watch that movie.
Let's memorize these words together.

grammar.explanation: Add ~읍시다 after a consonant and ~ㅂ시다 after a vowel (ㄹ stems drop the ㄹ: 만듭시다). It is a little more formal than ~자 and is typical of a boss addressing a team or coworkers talking to each other, but it can sound bossy toward someone senior.

examples.en: Let's start the meeting.
Let's take a short rest here.
Let's fill out this document today.
Let's recruit new employees next month.

grammar.point: ~ㄹ/을래요?: shall we? / do you want to?
grammar.explanation: Attach ~을래 after a consonant and ~ㄹ래 after a vowel, adding ~요 for politeness. As a question it asks whether the listener would like to do something, often together, and works with question words. Said with 맞다 or 혼나다 (맞을래?) it becomes an annoyed, empty threat.

examples.en: Shall we have coffee together?
What do you want to do on the weekend?
Do you want to watch a movie tonight?

grammar.explanation: Attached to 주다 or ~아/어 주다, ~ㄹ래요 makes a soft request rather than a direct command. Adding the honorific (~아/어 주실래요?) makes it even more polite, like "Could you please...".

examples.en: Could you open the door?
Can you turn on some music?
Could you please give this note to the teacher?

grammar.explanation: As a statement, ~ㄹ/을래요 says what the speaker wants or intends to do, similar to ~고 싶다 or the future tense. It is mostly used in short, simple sentences, and 안 or ~지 않을래요 expresses not wanting to.

examples.en: I'll have bibimbap.
I want to rest at home today.
I don't want to go.

vocab.en: to occur, to come up, to arise
to step aside, to step away

grammar.explanation: 수 is a dependent noun meaning roughly "way" or "ability", described by the verb with ~ㄹ (after a vowel) or ~을 (after a consonant). Adding 있다 says the ability or possibility exists, i.e. "can". It also forms questions and requests, often with ~아/어 주다 and 좀.

examples.ko: 저는 한국어를 유창하게 말할 수 있어요.
examples.en: I can speak Korean fluently.

examples.ko: 이 서류를 내일까지 작성할 수 있어요?
examples.en: Can you fill out this form by tomorrow?
Could you step aside a little?
You can refer to this book.

grammar.explanation: Replace 있다 with 없다 to say something is impossible or cannot be done. 이해할 수 없다 suggests something you fundamentally cannot understand, whereas 이해 못 하겠다 is more about not getting it right now.

examples.ko: 길이 미끄러워서 빨리 걸을 수 없어요.
examples.en: The road is slippery so I can't walk fast.

examples.ko: 기한이 지나서 환불을 받을 수 없어요.
examples.en: The deadline has passed so you can't get a refund.

examples.ko: 저는 그 사람의 행동을 이해할 수 없어요.
examples.en: I can't understand that person's behavior.

grammar.explanation: Only the final 있다/없다 changes for tense; the ~ㄹ/을 수 part stays the same. Use 있었다/없었다 for past ability and 있을 거예요/없을 거예요 for the future.

examples.ko: 어제는 일이 많아서 잘 수 없었어요.
examples.en: I couldn't sleep yesterday because I had a lot of work.
I will probably be able to go tomorrow.
I could swim when I was young.

grammar.explanation: Because 수 is a noun, particles can attach to it. ~가 (수가 없다) does not change the basic meaning but tends to add emphasis to the situation, like "just can't". The nuances of 수는 and 수도 come in later lessons.

examples.ko: 너무 웃겨서 웃음을 참을 수가 없어요.
examples.en: It's so funny I just can't hold back my laughter.
I really can't go right now.

examples.ko: 이 문제는 혼자 풀 수가 없어요.
examples.en: I just can't solve this problem alone.

lessons.title: Lesson 46: I have to/I need to ~아/어야 하다/되다/지/겠다, ~ㄹ 필요가 있다/없다

grammar.explanation: Add ~아야 (after ㅏ/ㅗ stems), ~어야 (other stems) or ~해야 (하다 words) and finish with 하다 or 되다; the two mean the same, though 되다 is more common in speech. The single Korean form covers English "must", "have to" and "should", so context decides the strength. Only the final 하다/되다 is conjugated for tense.

examples.en: I have to review this document by tomorrow.

examples.ko: 대학교에 가고 싶으면 열심히 공부해야 돼요.
examples.en: If you want to go to university, you should study hard.
I had to work late yesterday.
We will have to leave in 10 minutes.

grammar.explanation: In conversation 하다/되다 can be replaced by ~지 (polite ~죠), written attached to ~아/어야 with no space. It sounds like a natural spoken "of course I/you should".

examples.en: I should go home now.
If you're sick, you should take medicine.
To be healthy, you should exercise more.

grammar.explanation: ~아/어야 하겠다 is usually shortened to ~아/어야겠다. The speaker has just realized something from the situation and decides they had better do it, like "I guess I'd better...".

examples.en: It's late, so I'd better go now.
My eyesight got worse, so I guess I'll have to buy glasses.
I'd better get up earlier next time.

grammar.explanation: 필요하다 feels like a verb in English but is an adjective in Korean, so the thing that is needed takes ~이/가, not ~을/를.

examples.en: I need a new photocopier.
This work needs everyone's cooperation.
Do you need more time?

grammar.point: ~ㄹ/을 필요가 있다/없다: need to / don't need to
grammar.explanation: The noun 필요 (necessity) is described by a verb with ~ㄹ/을, then 있다 or 없다 is added: "there is (no) need to...". It is close to ~아/어야 하다, and the 없다 version is a common way to say something is unnecessary.

examples.ko: 이 문제를 다시 검토할 필요가 있어요.
examples.en: We need to look at this problem again.
There's no need to worry.
You don't need to come early tomorrow.

vocab.en: to stick out, to hold out

grammar.explanation: Add ~지만 directly to any verb or adjective stem (or 이다) to join two clauses that contrast: "A, but B" or "even though A, B". The first clause is presented as a known fact, which distinguishes it from ~아/어도. For past and future, attach it after ~았/었 or ~겠 / ~ㄹ 거 (갔지만, 가겠지만, 갈 거지만).

examples.en: This apartment is small but clean.
I like animals, but I can't raise one.
I was very sick, but I took part in the match.

examples.ko: 내일 비가 오겠지만 저는 갈 거예요.
examples.en: It will probably rain tomorrow, but I will go.

grammar.explanation: 그렇다 + ~지만 gives 그렇지만, used at the start of a sentence to mean "however" or "but even so" in reply to what was just said. It is a slightly more formal-sounding alternative to 하지만.

examples.en: However, I don't have time now.
Even so, I trust that person.

examples.ko: 그렇지만 차가 너무 커서 주차할 수 없어요.
examples.en: However, the car is too big, so I can't park it.

grammar.explanation: Add ~아도/~어도/~해도 to a stem to say the second clause happens no matter what happens in the first. Unlike ~지만, the first clause is a supposition that may or may not be true.

examples.en: Even if it rains, we will play the game.
Even if you're tired, you have to do your homework.
Even if it's half price, I won't buy it.

examples.ko: 그 사람은 많이 먹어도 살이 안 쪄요.
examples.en: Even if that person eats a lot, they don't gain weight.

grammar.explanation: Because the ~아/어도 clause is hypothetical, it can contain question words: 누가 ~아/어도 "whoever", 어디에 가도 "wherever", 뭘 해도 "whatever". 아무리 replaces 얼마나 to mean "no matter how much".

examples.en: No matter how busy you are, you have to eat.
No matter how much I study, I can't understand it.
Don't open the door, no matter who comes.
Wherever you go, there are a lot of people.

grammar.explanation: With nouns, 이다 becomes 이어도 or 이라도. After a vowel these shorten to ~여도 and ~라도.

examples.en: Even on weekends, I get up early.
Even if you are a student, you must follow the rules.
Even if you're the youngest, you have to do a lot of work.

grammar.explanation: 그렇다 + ~아/어도 gives 그래도, "even so" or "still", used to say the speaker's point holds despite the situation just mentioned.

examples.en: Even so, I am going.
Still, you have to do your homework.

examples.ko: 비가 많이 와요. 그래도 나가고 싶어요.
examples.en: It's raining a lot. Even so, I want to go out.

lessons.title: Lesson 49: There is no problem if: ~아/어도 되다

grammar.point: 되다: to work, to be OK, to be done
grammar.explanation: Besides "to become", 되다 can mean something is working, is going fine, or is finished. 안 되다 (not 못) says it isn't working or isn't possible, and 됐어요 can mean "that's enough".

examples.en: The computer isn't working well.
Dinner is all ready.
Tomorrow doesn't work for me.
That's enough. Please stop.

grammar.explanation: Combining ~아/어도 with 되다 literally means "even if you do it, it's fine", so it gives or asks permission: "you may" or "may I...?". 되다 can be put in the past or future for "it would have been / will be fine".

examples.en: May I sit here?
You may go home now.
Is it OK to take a picture?

examples.ko: 그 책은 내일 줘도 될 거예요.
examples.en: It will probably be fine to give me that book tomorrow.

grammar.explanation: Negate the verb with 안 or ~지 않아도 to say it is fine not to do something: "you don't have to". It is roughly the opposite of ~아/어야 하다.

examples.en: You don't have to go to school tomorrow.
You don't have to pay.
You don't have to worry.

grammar.explanation: 괜찮다 or 좋다 can replace 되다 with the same "it is OK if..." meaning, often sounding a little softer.

examples.en: Is it all right if I open the window?
Is it okay if I call now?
You can leave work early today.

grammar.explanation: The noun 예정 (schedule, plan) is described with the future modifier ~ㄹ/을, and 이다 finishes the sentence. It means something is scheduled or expected to happen and sounds a bit formal.

examples.ko: 저는 다음 달에 한국에 갈 예정이에요.
examples.en: I am scheduled to go to Korea next month.
The meeting is scheduled to start at three.

examples.ko: 그 섬에 대규모 호텔을 지을 예정이에요.
examples.en: They plan to build a large-scale hotel on that island.

grammar.explanation: 계획 (plan) is described the same way and followed by 있다, like English "have plans to". 없다 means having no such plans, and ~ㄹ/을 계획이다 is also used.

examples.ko: 저는 내년에 일을 그만둘 계획이 있어요.
examples.en: I have plans to quit my job next year.
Do you have plans to go to an island this summer?
I have no plans to get married.

grammar.explanation: 준비 (preparation) is described with ~ㄹ/을, and 되다 (to go well or be done) says whether the preparation is complete. It is usually in the past tense, 됐어요, meaning "is ready"; 안 됐어요 means "is not ready yet".

examples.en: I am ready to go now.
Are you ready to take the Korean SAT?
I am not ready to present yet.

grammar.explanation: With the active verb 하다, 준비 takes the object particle ~를. With an imperative ending it tells someone to "get ready to...", and it also describes getting ready in progress.

examples.en: Get ready to go out.
I am getting ready to leave now.
Hurry and get ready for bed.
